content: The impacts of wheelchair provision in Ethiopia were explored in a study published in the Journal of Development Effectiveness in 2016, which examined the outcomes of wheelchair distribution and its effectiveness in improving mobility and quality of life. Another study, published in Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology in 2022, emphasized the critical role of assistive technologies in achieving the goals of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, highlighting their importance in promoting accessibility and inclusion. A consumer assessment conducted in 2021, published in the Journal of Military, Veteran, and Family Health, focused on the experiences of women who use wheelchairs, providing insights into their satisfaction and challenges. Efforts to develop product quality standards for wheelchairs in resource-limited settings were detailed in a 2017 article in the African Journal of Disability. This study underscored the importance of durable and context-appropriate wheelchair designs. A Zimbabwean perspective on whether any wheelchair is better than none was presented in a 2015 study, which evaluated the functional and social impacts of wheelchair use in the region. Young people's experiences with electric-powered indoor-outdoor wheelchairs (EPIOCs) were explored in a 2007 study in Disability and Rehabilitation, which highlighted the potential of these devices to enhance user development. Similarly, a 2012 study in Pediatric Physical Therapy examined the effects of power wheelchairs on the development and function of young children with severe motor impairments, demonstrating significant benefits. The RESNA Position on the Application of Power Mobility Devices for Pediatric Users, published in 2017, provided guidelines for the appropriate use of power mobility devices in children. Additionally, a 2019 scoping review in Physical & Occupational Therapy in Pediatrics explored the use of modified ride-on cars as an early mobility intervention for children with mobility limitations. The World Population Prospects report by the United Nations in 2020 provided demographic insights relevant to assistive technology needs. A 2015 study in Age and Ageing examined the prevalence of frailty and disability in aging populations, emphasizing the growing demand for assistive devices like wheelchairs. The Global Burden of Disease Study 2017 highlighted the global impact of injuries and disabilities, further supporting the need for accessible assistive technologies. A 2019 study in the African Journal of Disability explored the use of Washington Group questions to identify individuals with clinical impairments who require assistive products, demonstrating the utility of population-based surveys in service delivery. The Wheelchair Provision Guidelines and related resources, such as the Priority Assistive Products List (APL), provide essential frameworks for ensuring equitable access to assistive devices. Research on wheelchair service provision has also focused on user satisfaction and functionality. For example, a 2016 study in Zimbabwe demonstrated the positive impact of structured wheelchair services on user satisfaction and functionality. Similarly, a 2018 study in Croatia assessed wheelchair users' satisfaction with prescribed devices and services, identifying areas for improvement. The UK Department of Health emphasized a whole-systems approach to wheelchair provision in a 2006 report, advocating for integrated services to promote independence. The relationship between prosthetics, orthotics, and community-based rehabilitation was explored in a 1999 joint statement by ISPO and WHO, highlighting the importance of interdisciplinary approaches. A 2018 study in Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology examined the role of appropriate personnel skill-mix in achieving equitable access to assistive technology, emphasizing the need for trained professionals. The experiences of individuals with physical disabilities during earthquakes were documented in a 2018 study, underscoring the importance of mobility aids in disaster preparedness. The inclusion of children with disabilities in disaster management was addressed in a 2021 study, which highlighted the need for tailored interventions. The Sphere Handbook provides minimum standards for humanitarian response, including considerations for assistive technology. National workforce capacity for implementing essential public health functions, including emergency preparedness, was outlined in a 2020 WHO roadmap. A 2016 review in Disability and Rehabilitation: Assistive Technology identified factors influencing wheelchair users' participation in social and community activities, emphasizing the role of mobility devices in promoting inclusion. A 2014 systematic review in BMC Health Services Research developed a conceptual framework for wheelchair interventions and services for disabled children, providing evidence-based recommendations. A 2018 evaluation in Canada examined policies governing funding for wheelchairs and scooters, identifying gaps in accessibility and equity. Sustainable solutions for wheelchair and seating assistive technology provision were presented in a 2014 study, advocating for a cosmopolitan narrative to address global disparities. The effectiveness of biomedical models in healthcare systems was questioned in a 2004 article in BMJ, calling for more holistic approaches. Barriers to mobility device access and implications for assistive technology reuse programs were discussed in a 2016 study, highlighting the need for policy reforms. The development of wheeled mobility indicators to improve spinal cord injury rehabilitation was detailed in a 2019 study, emphasizing the importance of standardized metrics. Peer-led wheelchair training programs have shown promise in improving self-efficacy and skills among users, as demonstrated in multiple studies. For example, a 2016 randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of a peer-led training program for manual wheelchair users, showing significant improvements in confidence and participation. The role of telehealth in delivering remote assessments for wheelchair and seating needs was explored in a 2020 scoping review, highlighting its potential to improve access to services. Similarly, a 2007 evaluation of wheelchair services in Afghanistan demonstrated the importance of context-specific interventions. An interdisciplinary approach to evaluating assistive technology needs was shown to reduce equipment abandonment, as reported in a 2006 study on multiple sclerosis. A 2017 survey in Kenya and the Philippines assessed wheelchair service outcomes, providing insights into user satisfaction and functionality. These studies collectively underscore the critical role of assistive technologies, particularly wheelchairs, in enhancing mobility, independence, and quality of life for individuals with disabilities. They also highlight the importance of evidence-based policies, interdisciplinary approaches, and user-centered service delivery models in achieving equitable access to these essential devices.
